rationale: A wins because it finds the most pitchable bottom-rung story: "Airbnb builds a travel-manager console to get short-term rentals written into company policy" turns a feature launch into a buyer problem with proof attached. B is good, but its lead angle, "Airbnb builds a managed-travel layer to compete for corporate bookings, not just vacations," jumps faster to incumbent conflict and leaves the travel manager as supporting cast. Drama is not a substitute for the person with the budget and the policy binder.
gaps_in_A: "a travel manager who has been fielding rogue Airbnb bookings on personal cards" is a plausible pain, not a supplied fact; keep it as a reporting question unless a customer will say it.
"Airbnb goes after managed corporate lodging spend with a tool it gives away" leans too hard on "free for travelers"; that does not prove the employer, host, or partner economics.
"Concur, the legacy expense system and a newer one" imports market color the update did not provide; useful if true, but it needs confirmation.

"Airbnb builds a travel-manager console" and "Airbnb goes after managed corporate lodging spend" partially share the same buyer-policy territory; keep both only if you can get customer proof and incumbent reaction.
gaps_in_B: "a direct play for budget that currently flows to hotel corporate rates and travel-management programs" asserts displacement the update does not prove.
"Expense software is becoming a travel distribution channel" is a smart angle, but it is too large a trend claim for two named integrations unless Concur, Ramp, or customers validate it.
It misses the cleanest customer-story angle as its own lane: the travel manager deciding whether Airbnb belongs in company policy.
"not just vacations" is a lazy contrast; the update says Airbnb is launching a business-travel product, not that its prior non-business demand was only vacations.
